newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan goes for growth as IMF suspends loan.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan goes for growth as IMF suspends loan.

text.p: Pakistan's Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz has promised a bold new strategy for export-led growth, but financial markets may react nervously to the suspension of an IMF standby loan, analysts said on Saturday.

They said the Karachi stock market was likely to plunge when it reopens on Monday while the rupee might slip in the kerb market after Friday's announcement that the International Monetary Fund standby arrangement had come to an abrupt end.
Aziz said foreign investors should take heart from what he said was an agreement with the IMF to bring forward negotiations on a softer medium-term loan to support structural adjustment.

"If they look at it in a broad context, in the sense that if our structural reform programme will improve the investment climate, reform the institutions, lighten the tax burden and create more incentives for exports, there should be a very good response from the investors," he told Reuters in an interview.
"And that, I hope, will improve our credit rating. Our reserves are already up from $600 million to $1 billion and hopefully in the next few weeks they'll improve even further."
An IMF mission that spent two weeks reviewing Pakistan's economic performance left on Friday without a public statement.
A finance ministry statement quoted the mission as welcoming the government's intention to implement structural reforms.

"It endorses the government's desire to move decisively to take radical measures for the reform of taxes and of tax administration as well as for accelerated privatisation and the revival of the industrial and agricultural sectors.

"The government's policy package, when implemented fully, will lay the basis for a transition to negotiations of a medium-term ESAF/EFF arrangement," it said, referring to IMF enhanced structural adjustment and extended fund facilities.
But analysts in Karachi said the collapse of the $830 million standby loan, of which the last $360 million was to have been disbursed by September, would still be seen as a blow.
"What could be worse?" asked Anisur Rehman, research head at SocGen-Crosby Securities, saying the 100-share index could slide to 1,400 or 1,450 points from Friday's 1,600.80-point close.
"This news is going to take the wind out of stocks for sure," Sameer Ahmed, sales head at ING Baring Securities, said.
Bankers said the risk attached to investment and lending to Pakistan would jump with no IMF programme in place. "Pakistan's cost of borrowing will skyrocket," said a foreign banker.

In November Moody's Investors Services cut Pakistan's sovereign ceiling for forex loans to B2 from B1/Not Prime and the ceiling for forex bank deposits to B3 from B2, keeping the latter rating under review for possible further downgrade.

Aziz said the IMF had ended the standby loan because slippages in revenue collection, particularly customs duties, made it impossible to meet the agreed target of cutting the budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product in 1996/97 (July-June) from 6.3 percent in 1995/96.
"The possibility of achieving that reduction in the budget deficit and improving the balance of payments was not possible unless the structural measures were taken," he said.
"So in a way we are now achieving the same results, with six or eight months' delay, but through a broader structural programme by broadening the tax base and...reviving the economy.
"We feel that if the economy is not revived, even if the standby programme is carried through absolutely to the last digit, the benefits would be limited," Aziz said.
Pakistan began a three-year ESAF programme with the IMF in February 1994, but then-prime minister Benazir Bhutto ended it in June 1995, saying her country needed breathing space.
A payments crisis later that year forced Pakistan to negotiate an IMF standby loan agreement, which was suspended in April 1996 because targets were not being met.

After another foreign exchange crunch in October last year, Bhutto's government announced a stabilisation package to get the IMF to resume the standby loan, but more talks were necessary after President Farooq Leghari sacked Bhutto on November 5.
The IMF resumed an expanded standby loan in December when a caretaker government was in power. The present government led by Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif took over after February 3 polls.
